title: Chapter XLVIII

teacherSummary.text: Mr. Collins sends a letter of 'condolence' saying Lydia's death would have been better. Mr. Bennet returns, admitting his fault but joking bitterly; Wickham's debts are exposed.

vocabulary.definition: (Physiol.) To pass off in the form of vapor or insensible perspiration
vocabulary.context: And in the wretched state of his own finances, there was a very powerful motive for secrecy, in addition to his fear of discovery by Lydia’s relations, for it had just transpired that he had left gaming debts behind him, to a very considerable amount.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “transpire”: trans- (Latin trans, "across"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Inclined to defer or put off what ought to be done at once
vocabulary.context: His family knew him to be on all common occasions, a most negligent and dilatory correspondent, but at such a time, they had hoped for exertion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dilatory”: -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state or quality of exceeding a measure or rule, or of being immoderate, monstrous, or outrageous
vocabulary.context: Bennet, I am inclined to think that her own disposition must be naturally bad, or she could not be guilty of such an enormity, at so early an age.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enormity”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To lighten or lessen the force or weight of

vocabulary.etymology: “disincline”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Moralizing letters were a social genre; Collins's is hypocritical.

discussionQuestions: Why is Collins's letter so offensive?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLVIII,” how does Austen show letters of judgment? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XLVIII, how does Austen develop the idea of letters of judgment? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVIII develops the idea of letters of judgment. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XLVIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of letters of judgment. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XLVIII suggests about letters of judgment. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XLVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of letters of judgment. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of letters of judgment responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XLVIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of letters of judgment follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XLVIII and its treatment of letters of judgment. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XLVIII as evidence for a larger claim about letters of judgment in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of letters of judgment. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: The whole party were in hopes of a letter from Mr. Bennet the next morning, but the post came in without bringing a single line from him. His family knew him to be on all common occasions, a most negligent and dilatory correspondent, but at such a time, they had hoped for exertion. They were forced to conclude that he had no pleasing intelligence to send, but even of that they would have been glad to be certain. Mr. Gardiner had waited only for the letters before he set off.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLVIII”?

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true
annotationFocus.passage: The whole party were in hopes of a letter from Mr. Bennet the next morning, but the post came in without bringing a single line from him. His family knew him to be on all common occasions, a most negligent and dilatory correspondent, but at such a time, they had hoped for exertion. They were forced to conclude that he had no pleasing intelligence to send, but even of that they would have been glad to be certain. Mr. Gardiner had waited only for the letters before he set off.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why is Collins's letter so offensive? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are transpired, dilatory, enormity, finances, alleviate. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “And in the wretched state of his own finances, there was a very powerful motive for secrecy, in addition to his fear of discovery by Lydia’s relations, for it had just transpired that he had left gaming debts behind him, to a very considerable amount.” Webster's says: (Physiol.) To pass off in the form of vapor or insensible perspiration. Now the word history: “transpire”: trans- (Latin trans, "across"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “dilatory”: -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “enormity”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Moralizing letters were a social genre; Collins's is hypocritical. Why does this chapter matter? Collins's cruel 'comfort' satirizes self-righteous religion. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to letters of judgment.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: The whole party were in hopes of a letter from Mr. Bennet the next morning, but the post came in without bringing a single line from him. His family knew him to be on all common occasions, a most negligent and dilatory correspondent, but at such a time, they had hoped for exertion. They were forced to conclude that he had no pleasing intelligence to send, but even of that they would have been glad to be certain. Mr. Gardiner had waited only for the letters before he set off.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLVIII,” how does Austen show letters of judgment? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about letters of judgment, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes letters of judgment. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
